source.title: Deep ConvNet: Non-Random Weight Initialization for Repeatable Determinism, Examined with FSGM †
source.citation: Richard N. M. Rudd-Orthner et al., 2021
source.authors: Richard N. M. Rudd-Orthner; L. Mihaylova

record.file_problem: Full published article text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Compares a proposed non-random weight initialization with random initialization and reports learning accuracy and loss. This bears conceptually on whether initialization changes learning speed, but it does not use the specific initialization methods or depth tests named in V4.
record.gate_note: Reports cross-validation accuracy and loss for different initializations and training durations. The text does not report training classification error or results on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100. Adversarial-transfer results are not included as rows because they measure transfer compromise rather than the initialization-speed or trainable-depth behavior in the versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses Glorot/Xavier and He initialization limits while evaluating its own deterministic weight sequences. It compares spatial arrangements and value distributions within those limits, rather than testing V4's activation-matched signal propagation, orthogonality, or trainable-depth claims. Faster fitting with its proposed initialization is a related finding, but does not establish the specific initialization effects in V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that their deterministic initialization improves early validation accuracy and reduces fitting loss faster under Xavier and He limits, including in a separate color-image architecture. They also report greater retention of original-data performance after adversarial retraining, accompanied by weaker performance on the retraining attack dataset.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a deterministic, structured non-random sequence for convolutional and dense-layer initialization and compares it with random initialization using Glorot/Xavier and He limits. It does not test the specific initialization interventions summarized in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset shuffling changes the reported benchmark accuracy; the first-epoch gain differs between shuffled and unshuffled training. The text also reports results with both Glorot/Xavier and He limits and on a separate MTARSI 2 architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed deterministic sequence improves MNIST first-epoch validation accuracy by 2.642–3.705 percentage points with Xavier limits and 4.27–5.13 points with He limits. Sections 4.2 and Figures 8–9 also explicitly report faster reduction of fitting loss with and without dataset shuffling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Structured deterministic initialization can accelerate early fitting relative to random sequences while retaining the same initialization limits in the tested convolutional networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Later MNIST validation advantages are smaller: 0.599 percentage points after five shuffled epochs with Xavier limits, and 0.70–1.83 points after two to five shuffled epochs with He limits.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The validation advantage of the proposed initialization diminishes over subsequent training epochs in the tested MNIST network.

fits_no_version.finding: On MTARSI 2, the proposed method achieves 54.69% versus 44.89% first-epoch validation accuracy, and 85.57% versus 82.28% at an unspecified later duration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed deterministic sequence improves validation accuracy in the tested color-image architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: After adversarial retraining with randomly varying perturbations, the proposed initialization retains higher original-data accuracy, 67.01% versus 61.05%, but has lower attack-data accuracy, 61.82% versus 78.41% (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization can affect the tradeoff between retaining original-task performance and adapting to adversarial retraining data.

record.problems: The reported training comparisons use cross-validation accuracy and loss, not training classification error. The benchmark and MTARSI 2 results do not state uncertainty estimates. The text presents some learning-loss comparisons only in figures, without exact values. The training durations for the MTARSI 2 accuracy comparison are not fully stated.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure-only learning-loss comparisons and adversarial-transfer results were not extracted because the figures provide no precise values and the transfer measures do not test the versioned initialization-speed or trainable-depth behaviors.

untested.parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random labels, model-size effects, and regularized or early-stopped recipes.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious local minima, and additional student neurons.
Training degradation with depth, identity shortcuts, very deep plain tanh networks, and Fixup.

Activation-matched initialization preserving signals and gradients, its effects on fitting speed and trainable depth, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights at matched variance, and 10,000-layer plain convolutional networks.
Stability thresholds, transient loss increases, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability training, and divergence.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and training without normalization using Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any version. The faster fitting-loss result is explicitly stated in the supplied text, although numerical curves are unavailable. It supports the proposed sequence's performance claim, not the specific mechanisms or depth comparisons in V4. Accuracy differences reported as gains are percentage-point differences.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, training classification error, random or corrupted labels, model size, and the stated training recipes are not tested.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and width variation are not tested.
Plain versus residual network depth and training error are not compared.

The study tests its own non-random initialization against random initialization, with first-epoch and later cross-validation accuracy and loss. It does not test Glorot/He activation-matched initializations as the intervention, signal or gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, very deep tanh networks, or 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
Learning rates above the stability limit, curvature, sharpness, and divergence are not tested.
Batch normalization, learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup are not tested.

reader_labels.condition: MNIST benchmark, first epoch, with Glorot/Xavier or He limits
reader_labels.reason: The proposed initialization has higher reported cross-validation accuracy than the random initialization in the first-epoch comparisons (R4, R5, R10, R11). This supports faster initial learning in these tested settings, though the measure is cross-validation accuracy rather than training error.
